title: Credit Building for Newcomers
subtitle: Turn financial experience into a documented Canadian credit path

blocks.text: You can arrive with years of responsible money habits and still get the Canadian credit version of “new phone, who is this?”

A thin Canadian file is a paperwork gap, not a flaw in your character. This course shows you how to keep your records, pick one reporting product, protect your due dates, keep reported balances low and check both bureau files. Do not collect applications like souvenir stamps.
Equifax and TransUnion build Canadian reports from activity reported in Canada. Foreign history does not turn into a Canadian file on its own, though some lenders may look at it.

items.title: “No Canadian score means I have bad credit.”
items.text: A thin or unscoreable file may just lack enough Canadian history. That is not the same as missed payments or too much debt.

blocks.text: FCAC: Credit-report and score basics
You can turn years of money habits into a Canadian file a lender can read.
blocks.detail: You will collect five steps in order, so a thin file stops being a verdict on you and becomes a gap you can close.
blocks.extra: Your first five passport stamps come next, then Amina’s story shows them at work.

blocks.text: A bank account keeps your everyday records, but it does not build a score on its own. A file starts when a reporting company sends in eligible account information.

items.title: STAMP 1 · PRESERVE EVIDENCE
items.text: Keep an international credit report if you can get one. Also keep bank reference letters, proof of income, rental records, savings history and current ID. Each lender decides what it accepts.

items.title: STAMP 2 · CHOOSE ONE PRODUCT
items.text: Ask whether it reports to Equifax, TransUnion or both. Compare the annual fee, interest, deposit, upgrade and cancellation terms before you apply.

items.title: STAMP 3 · PROTECT THE DUE DATE
items.text: Set alerts and an automatic minimum payment. Pay the full statement balance when you can afford it. A secured-card deposit is collateral, not a payment.

items.title: STAMP 4 · KEEP USE MODEST
items.text: FCAC suggests using less than 30% of your total available credit. Lower reported use may help, especially with a small limit.

items.title: STAMP 5 · VERIFY REPORTING
items.text: After a few update cycles, get both reports. Checking your own file is a soft inquiry and does not lower your score.

blocks.text: A secured card builds history only if the issuer reports it and you manage it well. The deposit does not erase interest, fees or missed payments.
An authorized user may spend on the card, but FCAC says those purchases do not build the user’s own credit history.

items.title: “Applying for several cards will build history faster.”
items.text: Several applications can mean several hard inquiries, fees and due dates. One affordable account that reports can build useful history.

sections.title: Amina’s File Was New; Her Habits Were Not

blocks.text: Meet Amina
paragraphs: Amina Yusuf moves to Winnipeg for a project-coordinator job. She brings savings, steady work and strong credit from abroad.
Her Canadian report is almost blank. It is the financial version of a freshly painted apartment: clean, promising and containing absolutely no furniture.
Then the pressure arrives. An apartment application asks for a score. A card is declined. Ads promise “instant Canadian credit” if she applies again and again.
Amina could apply everywhere. Instead she builds a Credit Passport: her international report, an employer letter, pay stubs, her lease, a bank reference and her ID.

She compares a newcomer card with a secured card. She asks which bureaus get the updates. Then she chooses one low-limit product. A small transit charge, payment alerts and an automatic minimum payment make a simple routine.
She pays in full, keeps reported use low and says no to store cards. After a few cycles, she checks both files.
The twist: one file shows the account. The other has her surname misspelled. She corrects it through the official process and keeps the confirmation.
At year-end there is no big score reveal. There is a steady Canadian file, her international papers kept safe and no pile of beginner products.
Her file was new. Her habits were not.

blocks.text: Amina protected one account long enough for accurate Canadian history to build.
What resolved the conflict?
One reporting path, reliable documents and scheduled bureau checks replaced the rush to apply with a plan she could repeat.
You can catch a wrong spelling before it costs you a loan.
blocks.detail: You will check both reports on a schedule, so an error is found by you and not by a lender.
blocks.extra: Next, the roadmap turns Amina’s routine into a 12-month calendar.

blocks.text: Move forward on evidence, not on score chasing.

items.title: DAYS 1–30 · SET THE BASE
items.text: Open basic banking, learn the fees, make a payment calendar and keep your records from abroad. Do not buy optional products just because “newcomer” is on the brochure.

items.title: MONTHS 1–3 · OPEN CAREFULLY
items.text: Pick one reporting product after you compare the cost, limit, deposit, bureau reporting and the cancel or upgrade rules.

items.title: MONTHS 3–6 · CREATE A CLEAN PATTERN
items.text: Make every required payment on time, keep use modest and do not borrow just to make the account look busy.

items.title: MONTHS 6–12 · AUDIT AND PREPARE
items.text: Review both reports, fix errors and keep proof. For a major loan, bring income, savings and international-credit evidence.

blocks.text: CMHC newcomer guidance allows other evidence of creditworthiness in some cases. That can include an international report or a financial-institution reference. Full underwriting still applies.

items.title: “A foreign credit score converts directly into the same Canadian score.”
items.text: Canadian bureaus use Canadian activity. Some lenders may review foreign reports or references, but there is no shortcut that converts one score into another.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: What is the difference between a thin Canadian file and poor credit?
items.detail: A thin file lacks enough reported Canadian history. A poor file shows negative behaviour, such as missed payments or too much debt.

items.title: What should you check before you choose a newcomer or secured card?
items.detail: The fees, interest, deposit rules, limit, cancel or upgrade terms and whether it reports to Equifax, TransUnion or both.

items.title: Does a secured-card deposit replace the monthly payment?
items.detail: No. The deposit protects the issuer. You still owe the card bill.

items.title: Why is one manageable product often stronger than several applications?
items.detail: It can build useful history with fewer inquiries, fees and due dates.

items.title: Which records may help a lender assess limited Canadian history?
items.detail: International reports, bank references, income, savings, rental records and current ID, depending on the lender’s policy.

blocks.text: CMHC: Newcomers
Write document names and partial references only. Leave out SINs, passwords, PINs, immigration document numbers and full account numbers.
Your passport shows one useful account, protected due dates, modest use and both reports reviewed.
A new Canadian file does not mean new financial habits.
blocks.detail: Keep your international evidence, choose one affordable Canadian reporting product, protect every due date, keep use modest and check both reports before you go after larger credit.

items.title: Thin file
items.text: A credit file with too little reported information for a solid lending decision or a score.

items.title: Reporting product
items.text: A credit account whose issuer sends account information to one or both Canadian credit bureaus.

items.title: Secured credit card
items.text: A card backed by a security deposit. You still owe the monthly balance.

items.title: Credit utilization
items.text: The reported card balance compared with the available credit limit.

items.title: Hard inquiry
items.text: A lender’s credit check linked to an application. It may affect your score.

items.title: Soft inquiry
items.text: A credit check, such as looking at your own report, that does not affect your score.
